title: Back to the Future
synopsis: Hill Valley, 1985. The DeLorean. The lightning. You end up in 1955, where your mother has a crush on you. Don't break the timeline.

nodes.text: One in the morning, empty car park, and Doc's dog goes a minute into the future and comes back with his tail wagging and his watch running late. Doc is still whooping about it when a van comes across the tarmac with men in it who want their plutonium returned. Doc goes down. You are in a stainless steel car with no plan, and the trick needs eighty-eight miles an hour.

choices.consequence: You get the door shut, find reverse, and take a lap of the car park with a van on your bumper and no idea what the fuel gauge means.
You make it nine steps before remembering the men have automatic weapons and you have a skateboard, and you turn round and sprint for the car.

nodes.text: You come out of the flash still doing eighty-eight, in a cornfield, in daylight, and stop inside a barn. Silver car. Radiation suit. A farm family in dressing gowns stares at you over a lantern. The father goes for the shotgun. Their small son is holding a comic about invaders from space and having, visibly, the greatest night of his life. A pine tree does not survive the exit.

choices.consequence: You pull the hood off and start explaining the barn, the car and the year, which somehow makes the shotgun come up faster.
You reverse through the barn doors while a farmer fires into the air and a kid yells at you to come back next Thursday.

nodes.text: The square has a working fountain, a cinema showing a cowboy picture, and a clock tower keeping perfect time. Every hat matches every other hat. In the middle of all this civic pride, a skinny kid is being shoved from behind by a tall boy with a laugh like a car alarm, while grown men step politely around them. The skinny kid has your surname.

choices.consequence: You put yourself between them without saying anything clever, and the tall boy looks at you like a vending machine that just spoke.
You stand at the kerb with your hands in your pockets and watch your father pick his books out of a puddle by himself.

nodes.text: You ask for a soft drink with no sugar in it and Lou looks at you the way a man looks at a request for credit. Behind you the tall boy has your father's head down on the counter and wants his homework by Monday. Every stool in the place is watching and nobody moves. You are thirty years early for every single thing you want to say.

choices.consequence: You buy the drink, sit at the counter, and learn the name of the man who will be signing your father's paycheques for three decades.
You leave before you say something you cannot afford, and walk out past a boy with your jaw and your posture and none of your luck.

nodes.text: Your father goes out of the tree he was up, into the road, and you shove him clear and take the bumper yourself. You come round on a floral couch under a crocheted blanket, being addressed as Calvin, because that is the name printed on the waistband of your underwear. A girl of seventeen is sitting rather close with a cold cloth. She is your mother.

choices.consequence: You answer in short polite sentences and keep both hands where everyone can see them, which she finds mysterious and extremely attractive.
You try being friendly and normal, and she takes friendly and normal as tremendous encouragement, and moves eight inches closer.

nodes.text: Young Doc has a colander of wiring strapped to his head, a chalkboard of dead ends, and no interest in visitors. Then you say flux capacitor, and hand him a sketch he drew an hour ago after falling off a toilet and hitting his head. He goes silent. Then very loud. Then he wants to know everything about the future, beginning with who ends up President.

choices.consequence: You tell him the lot — the wars, the cars, the actor in the White House — and he sits down on the steps and stops arguing.
You give him the engineering and nothing else, and he keeps circling back to the year, the way a man picks at a scab.

nodes.text: Hill Valley High smells of floor polish and dread. Your father hides in a stairwell writing stories about creatures from other planets that he will never let anybody read, and cannot get through a whole sentence aimed at a girl. Meanwhile the clock runs: your parents have to meet, dance, and kiss on Saturday, or you start going transparent from the fingers inwards.

choices.consequence: You spend three lunch hours teaching a shy boy how to walk across a room, and he practises on a locker with reasonable success.
You skip the confidence-building and go straight to arranging it, which means the plan now depends on two people who have never spoken.

nodes.text: You get him to the diner, sit him in a booth, and make him rehearse the invitation on a napkin until it sounds like English. He crosses the floor. He gets four words out. Then the tall boy's car pulls up outside and your father turns into a coat rack. So it needs a middleman now — a seventeen-year-old pitching a romance to his own dad.

choices.consequence: You promise him it will work and shake his hand on it, and he believes you completely, which is the most frightening part of the afternoon.
You scrap the whole approach and start again on paper, with a diagram, at a table, like a man planning a bank job.

nodes.text: She gets there first. She corners you by the lockers with a directness nobody thought to warn you about and asks you to the dance on Saturday. She also smokes, keeps a flask, and disapproves out loud of girls who chase boys. Your plan now requires you to be your mother's date on Saturday night, and then somehow, urgently, stop being it.

choices.text: Pretend to fall in love with her
choices.consequence: You say yes and start building an elaborate scheme where your father heroically interrupts, which requires everyone to hit their marks perfectly.
You try telling her the truth in a hallway, get three sentences in, and hear how completely deranged it sounds out loud.

nodes.text: The tall boy corners your father behind the diner with three friends and a lot of enthusiasm. You choose volume: an insult, a sprint, and a child's scooter with the box torn off it. Their car chases you around the square at twenty miles an hour, full of shouting, and finishes nose-down in a truck full of manure. The whole square applauds. Twice.

choices.consequence: You get in the boot of a parked car to hide, which seems clever for about four seconds and then turns out to have a lid.
You go over a bonnet and down an alley, and arrive at the dance with a scraped shin and no idea where anyone is.

nodes.text: Parked outside the gym, she produces a flask, a cigarette and a plan, and none of your script survives contact. She kisses you. Then she stops, sits back, and says with real bewilderment that it felt wrong — like kissing a brother. You have never in your life been so grateful to be found unappealing by another human being.

choices.consequence: You file it as a data point: the timeline is repairing itself, and the photograph in your pocket has stopped losing people for a minute.
You slump against the door and laugh out of pure relief, and she takes it badly, which is somehow still an improvement.

nodes.text: The door is pulled open and a hand the size of a dinner plate takes you out of the car and drops you into the boot of the one behind it. The lid comes down. The tall boy gets in with your mother. Inside the boot with you is a saxophone case, and outside it is a band who would quite like their car back.

choices.consequence: You spend eleven seconds working out the physics of the lock, then give up and start hammering on the lid with a shoe.
You put your back against the spare tyre and kick until something metal gives, and come out onto the gravel bleeding from one knuckle.

nodes.text: Your father arrives to perform the rescue you wrote for him and finds an actual one instead: wrong man, real fear, his girl shouting. Everybody stops. His fist comes up and goes out, and he looks more astonished than anyone. One punch. A boy who has spent seventeen years apologising for taking up space is standing over the town bully in a car park.

choices.consequence: You get out of the way and let him walk her inside, and he does not once look back to check whether you approved.
You whoop from the gravel like a man at a ball game, which nobody hears, and which you would not have missed for anything.

nodes.text: Inside, the band is playing something slow and your parents are standing four feet apart looking at the floor. Meanwhile your hand is going see-through — first in the photograph in your pocket, then in the actual room, where you can read a poster through your own knuckles. The guitarist has cut his hand open. They need someone who knows the song.

choices.consequence: You pick up a guitar with fingers you can partly see through, and the tuning takes longer than it should because your hand keeps flickering.
You stay against the wall willing two teenagers to move, and the song ends, and nothing happens, and the next song starts.

nodes.text: You start clean and it is fine and the floor fills up. Then the fade goes long, and you drift forward a decade or two: a knee slide, a kicked amplifier, a solo with actual violence in it. The dancing stops. Four hundred teenagers in cardigans watch with the polite, total incomprehension of people being shown next Tuesday.

choices.consequence: You wind it back, land the last chord clean, and hand the guitar over with the dignity of a man who has borrowed something.
You go up on the amp anyway and finish it howling, and one boy at the back writes down every single thing you did.

nodes.text: Doc has a cable strung from the tower to a lamp post, a hook bolted to the car roof, and a bolt of lightning that will land at a moment every person in this town has known for thirty years. Tolerance is about a quarter of a second. He is out on a ledge in the wind with a length of chain, absolutely delighted with himself.

choices.consequence: You take the wheel and pace out the run twice with a stopwatch, because a quarter of a second is not a thing you improvise.
You make him walk the whole sequence again on the chalkboard, and he loves it, because nobody has ever asked him to explain anything twice.

nodes.text: You write it in the diner on the back of a bill: the date, the mall car park, the van, the men, wear something under your coat. He finds it in his pocket, reads two lines, and tears it into small pieces without finishing. There are rules about a man knowing his own future, he says, and hands you the pieces back.

choices.consequence: You tape it back together in the dark, fold it into his coat pocket while he is on the roof, and hope he is untidy.
You try saying it out loud instead, and he puts his hands over his ears in the street like a man refusing a dessert menu.

nodes.text: The cable comes loose at the worst possible moment. Doc goes down the tower on a rope with the grip of an enthusiastic amateur, reconnects it with the hook already coming, and you are flat out at eighty-eight with a wire dead ahead. The bolt lands on schedule. Everything goes white, the road behind you empties out, and the year on the dash reads 1985.

choices.consequence: You hold the line dead straight and let the car do the rest, which is the hardest thing you have done all week.
You bury the pedal at the last second and take the hook at speed, and the engine dies the moment the light lets go of you.

nodes.text: The mall sign says Lone Pine now, and the car stalls out and sits smoking on the tarmac. You run a mile in unhelpful shoes and arrive in time to watch the van, the shouting, the shots, the fall — all of it again, from the front row this time. Then the man on the ground sits up, opens his jacket, and shows you a vest and a taped-up letter.

choices.consequence: You get there flat out with your lungs burning and your legs gone, and see him drop, and it is worse the second time.
You hang back behind a parked car with your hands over your mouth, and the whole thing plays out exactly as it did before.

nodes.text: Your house smells of good coffee. Your father has a first novel and a box of author copies on the table and cannot stop touching them. Your mother is funny, fit, and did not marry a man who apologises for breathing. Your brother wears a suit that fits. And out front, the town bully is waxing the family car and calling your dad sir.

choices.consequence: You walk through every room touching things, checking, and find your own school photos on a wall you do not recognise.
You sit down, take the coffee, and let a family you have never actually met feed you breakfast without asking a single question.

nodes.text: You are about two minutes into an ordinary morning when the car drops onto your street in a cloud of steam with Doc in silver sunglasses tipping a bin bag of banana skins into a hopper on the back. He is talking very fast about your children and something that happens to them. He wants both of you in the car now, engine running, immediately.

choices.consequence: You get in with no shoes on and no explanation for Jennifer, and the street drops away underneath the wheels before you have found the belt.
You tell him you will need an hour, and he stares at you as though hours were a thing a time machine could be bothered by.
You ask him what he wants to build next, and he stops mid-sentence, and it is the first time in his life anybody has asked.

nodes.text: You go to 2015, sort out something regrettable involving your own son, and come home with a sports almanac problem you will be arguing about for years. Eventually you stop travelling. You marry Jennifer in a garden. You end up a parent yourself, with a boy who slams doors, and you find you are a fraction more patient than your father was — mostly because you have met him at seventeen and know exactly how hard it was.

You let Doc go on alone and wave at a car that is no longer on the road. Then you go inside and have breakfast with a family you accidentally improved. You finish school. You get a job you can stand. On Friday nights you play guitar in a four-piece at a bar off the square, and once a year you drive out to the Peabody farm and buy a pine sapling from a very old man who still remembers a silver car.

You and Doc work together for thirty years in a garage that smells of solder and burnt coffee. You never mass-produce anything, mostly because he refuses to make the same object twice. There is a clock that runs on tides, a coffee machine with a mind of its own, and one car nobody is allowed to look under. People drive across three states to stand in your doorway, and he charges them nothing.
